subject: 2000 S Geneva Rd gas-station rezone
comment: My wife and I have owned our home on 322 W 1750 North for the past 20 years. We are deeply opposed to any project on the State Street Corridor at 1600 N. that would affect our traffic (on 400 W or the intersections at 1600 N), parking on 400 W, or the crime rates in this area. We do not think sufficient attention is being given to these factors with the currently proposed apartments at the 1600 N 400 W location. When the State Street Corridor was approved, the incredibly tiny space at that corner was thought small enough that only small businesses or housing could be put in there. We assumed no housing along 400 W could be re-zoned, and certainly no access from 400 W would be granted to any properties there. Now we see that these very things are being considered and we are very upset. There is simply no space for any such building on the corner of 1600 N 400 W if the last house on 400 W remains as currently zoned. We are also deeply concerned about the likelihood of the proposed housing being turned into Section 8 housing before or soon after completion. That seems to be something developers/owners have done in the past in order to get additional credits and other payouts. All in all, this side of the corridor being so close to our homes should not be allowed to have such high-density housing. I recommend that the city council not approve any variances from current zoning at all, and that the city council examine traffic and parking in more detail around such a project. Jason Bench mentioned in a recent meeting that a gas station was once considered for this same space, and the traffic for this new housing project wouldn't be any worse than the gas station. I disagree with that thinking. Gas stations do not attract traffic. They are a stop of convenience for people already leaving or coming through that area. The fact that a gas station was once considered should not be used to justify the traffic and parking problems the proposed building and commercial use would create. In summary, my wife and I are opposed to this project because of the likely traffic, parking, crime impact, and potential for Section 8 approval that would follow. We call on all city council members to change the Corridor Zoning in whatever way necessary to prevent such out-of-place proposals from ever being built so close to single-family residential areas.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: We, the residents of the neighborhood along 400 West adjoining the State Street, North Village District, wish to convey our concerns about the proposed North Village District zone changes. We understand that the fifty-foot setback limiting the height of new developments along 400 West is a positive change to help limit the impact and flow from a commercial area to the residential area. However, we are concerned that not enough is being done to help this problem. The North Orem neighborhoods are much quieter and less commercial than other areas of Orem City, such as the City Center District, the Hub District, The Canyon Crossing District, and even the Arts District Zones. We fear that, as developments begin to build in this area, the quiet, safe neighborhood we love is in jeopardy. Many families have resided in these neighborhoods for decades and include multi-generations from aged parents to small children, for which we have special concerns. Therefore, we are asking that our concerns be considered before any decisions are made. The houses that are currently located in the North Village District that are zoned as NVD-Res(B) and the other homes located along 400 West should be more protected from encroaching developments. We feel the fifty-foot setback that is proposed is insufficient and request it be extended to seventy-five or even 100 feet from 400 West street. This would ensure that we have an adequate buffer in the heights allowed in the edge zone immediately next to our neighborhood. In addition, we feel that these homes located in this North Village District should have the setback for height restrictions measured from their backs and sides of the properties to prohibit excessively high buildings being built directly behind their properties rather than the setback being measured from the curb in front of the property (400 West). We also believe that it would be prudent to change these homes out of the North Village District and back to their original R-zone status to protect the neighborhood from the encroaching businesses and large multifamily developments. We realize that it is sensible for Orem to continue to grow and do not oppose growth itself. However, in this area of Orem we residents encourage growth that does not call for excessively high buildings. We understand that, since the North Village District is the smallest of the state street districts, it does not have a minimum height requirement. On the other hand, we believe that a maximum height limit should be set to prevent these neighborhoods, agreeable blends of well-crafted, established older homes and new homes from being overshadowed by multi-storied, multi-family buildings. We have no problem with State Street and its attendant business and apartment buildings reflecting the vibrant, metropolitan side of Orem City; we just ask the City Planning Commission and other concerned parties to respect and appreciate the value of established, quiet, and safe neighborhoods to the city as well. We also feel the need to address other concerns we have regarding the possibility of a large multi family unit being built in the area of 1600 North and 400 West. Increased traffic in this area is not acceptable. The streets are narrow and the space between State Street and 400 West is so short that if an entrance to a large multifamily development were built, it would create traffic congestion affecting two already busy intersections. The 1600 North corridor is very narrow; traffic moves very fast; and the safety of drivers and pedestrians is of great concern to us. This development could also make turning left onto 400 West from eastbound 1600 North even more difficult considering the fact that 400 West is a collector road that connects to Lindon and Pleasant Grove. It should be noted that we anticipate a substantial increase in traffic resulting from the establishment of a new LDS temple on north 2000 in Lindon. That will be difficult enough, but the increase in congestion as a result of the apartment complex will hardly be tolerable and will be extremely detrimental to our neighborhoods. The surrounding smaller streets, 280 West in particular, would likely see an increase in traffic and congestion issues as well. In addition, potential overflow parking from the project considered would inevitably spread to 400 West. The street is not wide enough to accommodate cars parked along it and would create traffic congestion and safety concerns, particularly in the unfinished portions along the west side. A number of residents who attended previous meetings regarding this project feel that they were misled, and certain requests were disregarded. The State Street Master Plan in 2015 did NOT include the homes in the zoning changes. Open houses and city-held charrettes indicated the zoning for the homes would remain unchanged. Again, this was misled

subject: Hillcrest park / greenspace
comment: I was recently made aware of the proposals for the Hillcrest property. I am writing to ask that the city take advantage of this unique opportunity that Orem has to increase our available green space with this piece of land. Please don’t put in more pickle ball courts. The pickle ball courts only appeal to a small percentage of the residents of Orem. It is unfair to take one of the few available spaces left in the city and use it entirely for a small subset of the population, those who would be interested in having enough pickle ball courts for a tournament. Orem needs outside space that will attract kids, tweens, teenagers, and families. We need space that allows outdoor activities for all different age groups. What we need are splash pads and skate parks, a bike track and shade trees, places for picnics and open areas for pick up soccer and football games. Please consider the needs of the entire city when making this decision, and don’t cater to the select few who think that the pickle ball courts we already have all over the city aren’t enough. Please remember all the residents of Orem when deciding what to do with this valuable space. Thank you.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate the Council's consideration in implementing a 50' setback from the back property line of homes in the Res-B zone of the North Village District and adjacent residential zones. Zoning efforts to buffer residents from commercial property is crucial in maintaining desirable and higher value residential property. It is my request that the City Council consider increasing this setback from 50' to 100' wherever a NVD-E (Edge Zone) abuts a residential zone. Edge zones are designed for mixed commercial/residential use, with building heights restricted by parking and setback requirements. There are many cases in the North Village District where Edge Zones abut R8 zones. It is my understanding that mid-density Res-B zones are transition zones to step down from commercial to standard residential zones. Many standard residential zones of the North Village District abut Edge Zones and do not have Res-B zones as a transition, which allows taller commercial/high-density housing to be built right next to an R8 zone. Increasing the setback from 50' to 100' where ALL residential zones abut an Edge Zone would protect and buffer residential properties that do not have a Res-B zone as a transition. Although not on today's agenda, I would further propose that certain Edge Zones be considered for rezoning to Res-B, especially where they abut R8 zones. One such property is between State Street and 400 W (behind State Street Storage and continues to the corner of 1600 N and 400 W) which does not have State Street frontage - not ideal for the required commercial element of an Edge zone property. The current Res-B homes along 400 W have applied to be rezoned back to R8. If this application is approved, rezoning the current Edge Zones behind it and to the south (corner of 1600 N & 400 W) to Res-B would provide the transition from commercial to residential, as well as provide a better use for a property that is currently zoned mixed commercial/residential with no State Street frontage or access. I understand that a lot of time and resources have gone into preparing the Master Plan. However, now is a good time to take another look and improve upon the Master Plan for the North Village District. The Master Plan states, "The NVD zones are intended to be more residential in nature, with neighborhood retail and smaller-scale development compared to the other four State Street Districts” (Ord. No. O-2018- 0029, Enacted 10/9/2018). Increasing Edge Zone setbacks to 100' and rezoning some Edge and Res-B zones, is in keeping with the Master Plan description of the North Village District and would be beneficial to all Orem City residents involved. Thank you for your time and consideration.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: City Council & City of Orem As stated in the Orem City “Code of Ordinances” (Article 22-24- 5), “Purpose. The North Village District (NVD) zones are located at the City’s northern gateway. The NVD zones are intended to be more residential in nature, with neighborhood retail and smaller-scale development compared to the other four State Street Districts.” (Ord. No. O-2018- 0029, Enacted 10/9/2018) As a resident whose property abuts the North Village District, I want to thank the Commission and Council for considering the impact of commercial and high-density development on residential areas. The recent proposal to create a 50’ setback around the NVD- ResB zone is a great example of this. Upon further review of the NVD ordinances, I have a few concerns and requests: • Residential Rezoning – The NVD-E and NVD-ResB zones are designed to scale back larger development as it nears residential, transitioning from commercial to mid- density residential. There has been a request submitted to change the current NVD-ResB zone along 400 W back to RES-8. If this is approved, it would make sense to rezone the portion of NVD-E adjacent to the west and south of this area to NVD-ResB. With it currently zoned NVD- E, it requires some commercial/residential mix. Changing a portion of the NVD-E zone (corner of 400 W and 1600 N as well as the area behind the homes on 400 W) to NVD-ResB with a 35’ maximum building height, would allow the stepdown from commercial to mid-density housing, as zoning ordinances are designed to do. o Benefits – Changing a portion of the NVD-E zone to NVD-ResB would allow a developer to build mid-density housing in an area that already has residential nearby without the commercial restrictions. This would alleviate some of the residents’ concerns with commercial areas creeping into the residential. State Street access is limited in this area and eliminating the commercial aspect of this property would help with easement from other surface streets. • Property Line Setback Requirements – Although the 50’ setback behind the homes on 400 W is a great improvement, 50’ is not very much room to buffer from larger buildings. It would be a huge benefit to all residents near the North Village District to have this setback requirement increased to 100’ wherever NVD-E abuts a Res-8 zone without the NVD-ResB as a stepdown buffer. My home (RES-8) at 399 W 1560 N, is such a property that currently has NVD-E on the back fence line. Without doing any rezoning, increasing the 50’ setback to 100’ would help buffer from any further, large developments. • Street Setback Requirements – Currently, the ordinance is to have any new build be 10’ from the sidewalk. As this may work for State Street, it is not conducive to 1600 N or other streets in this district. Having large buildings within 10’ of the sidewalk, or less, on 1600 N does not help with the residential feel as it transitions to residential areas. The “corridor” or “boulevard” look and feel should be focused on State Street only in the North Village District. • Commercial/Residential Access – Allowing any connector streets from commercial businesses or State Street to 400 W would only contribute to the existing congestion. Maps show future plans for the North Village District with a connector road cutting through the area between 1600 N and 1800 N. The residents do not support any roads going through, and request that any commercial or higher density housing traffic be directed toward State Street and not 400 W. • Maximum Building Height – In keeping with the purpose of the NVD zone, “with neighborhood retail and smaller- scale development compared to the other four State Street Districts,” it only makes sense to limit building height in this area. The NVD-E zones currently do not have a maximum building height but are restricted by other ordinances (parking and setback requirements). In the NVD-ResB zone building height maximum is 35’. Creating a 50’ maximum height in the NVD-E zones would provide a clearer transition from larger NVD-C developments and protect the property values of neighboring NVD-ResB or R8 zones. • Parking – Currently the NVD-E ordinance of 1.75 parking stalls is insufficient. Limiting parking in these residential/commercial zones means that surface streets are used as overflow. The surface streets cannot handle any more congestion, whether parked or moving. The theory that mixed residential/commercial will share parking, with commercial use during the day and residential at night, may not be the case as we move forward through and out of the pandemic. Many businesses have stated that working from home will be a viable option even once the pandemic is over. More people will be home during the day, with their cars parked in these shared residential/commercial stalls. Now is a great time to address the ordinance and to increase parking requirements to at least 2 stalls per unit. All of these ordinance and zoning changes would benefit the residents of the North Village District, as well as Orem City as a whole. Creating and maintaining a more defined and separate commercial, high-density housing, and protected residential zones, makes for a better aesthetic and functioning city. Traffic is already a major issue in Orem, with the NVD not an exception. These changes would help alleviate further congestion and provide a safer place for residents. After all, the NVD zones “are intended to be more residential in nature, with neighborhood retail and smaller-scale development compared to the other four State Street Districts (Ord. No. O- 2018-0029, Enacted 10/9/2018).” It is time to revisit the Master Plan to continue to protect residential areas from commercial and high-density housing development. Thank you for your time and consideration into these matters.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate the Council's consideration and support and at this time I ask City Council to consider increasing this setback from 50' to 100' wherever a NVD-E (Edge Zone) abuts a residential zone. Edge zones are designed for mixed commercial/residential use, with building heights restricted by parking and setback requirements. Many standard residential zones of the North Village District abut Edge Zones and do not have Res-B zones as a transition (for example homes behind Mountain America Bank), which allows taller commercial/high-density housing to be built right next to an R8-zone. Currently, all seven residents on 400 West have applied to change homes from Res-B (who were not aware of this change) along 400 West back to R8-zone homes which they should have never changed in the first place. All who are asking council members and the city to approve their request in a future time, and if this application is approved, it would facilitate the rezoning of the current Edge Zone behind it to Res-B. This would provide the transition from commercial to residential, as well as provide a better use for a property that is essentially landlocked. Increasing the setback from 50' to 100' where ALL residential zones abut an Edge Zone would protect and buffer residential properties. Furthermore, it would lessen the impact on the traffic that is already dangerous and impacting residential neighborhoods. A dangerous example of insufficient setbacks is Quick-Quack which was built right at the corner of 1600 North so close to residential homes, our neighborhoods recently experience dangerous driving conditions and traffic chaos due to enormous lines and blocked traffic. As many of you know traffic in this area is not an isolated event and the amount of traffic on 400 West and at the intersection of 1600 North and 400 West is at times dangerous. The number of accidents that have occurred at this intersection and on 400 West has been significant with people driving over 40 miles per hr. I also request, that due to the amount of traffic, that no roads or connecting streets go through 400 W from any commercial or higher density housing. I understand that a lot of time and resources have gone into preparing the Master Plan. However, now is a good time to take another look and improve upon the Master Plan for the North Village District. The Master Plan states, "The NVD zones are intended to be more residential in nature, with neighborhood retail and smaller-scale development compared to the other four State Street Districts.” (Ord. No. O-2018-0029, Enacted 10/9/2018) Increasing Edge Zone setbacks to 100' and rezoning current Edge and Res-B zones, is in keeping with the Master Plan description of the North Village District and would be beneficial to all Orem City residents involved.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate the work that went into creating the State Street Master Plan and the ideas put forth to help beautify development along State Street. The residents in my area feel the North Village District has some unique issues & request that zoning adjustments be made to address those issues. 1- There is NO Buffer Zone for the homes on 400 West, there should be a transitional RES (B) type zone between the State street Core Zone and the homes on 400 West. The Edge zone is not a sufficient buffer and a Res(B) zone designation would be more appropriate up to the1800 North boundary. The Res(B) zone would be in keeping with the purpose of this node. As stated in the State Street Master Plan, it is ‘intended to be more residential in nature’. Please rezone the inner section on the Northeast node to a medium density "condo-type" housing or small commercial/office with customary density and height. 2- Height restrictions for the property directly behind the homes should be revised and the 50 ft setback should be increased to 75-100 feet. The height of buildings should transition down from State Street, not from the middle of the node or from 1600 North. The land behind and to the south side of the homes should have Res(B) height restrictions. The homes need a buffer greater than 50 feet -- 75 or 100 feet would be in keeping with similar transitions found in other areas of Orem where medium density housing abuts to single family housing. 3- Building setbacks should be more than 0-10 feet from the curb, and the shoulders on 1600 North should be increased to the customary width found on other large collector streets. Eastbound 1600 North has extremely narrow shoulders on the North and South sides. Several times an accident or local business travel have created extreme traffic issues for residents as 1600 North is a main transportation gateway for the North Orem area. Zoning setbacks that will allow for an opportunity to widen 1600 North to 400 West would be wise and would reduce future costs and problems. A wider shoulder between the street and the sidewalk will provide greater safety for pedestrians. A walkable community provides for the safety of pedestrians and that area is not safely walkable. 4- A requirement for businesses to provide a few street visible parking spots would provide a safer, more visible parking area for women verses all parking in the back behind the building. I had an unsettling experience once where a man approached me in a parking lot that was secluded behind a building. I was grateful the business had a security guard patrolling the parking lot. Requiring a few parking options in front would provide a safe option for those seeking one. Please consider this for State Street. Thank you for helping us to preserve our neighborhoods and the safety of our streets.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate the fine people in the planning commission and their willingness to meet with the neighbors near the North Village District to help us understand how the city processes work. These planning people are our neighbors and friends. I am excited to have my home, one of the homes on the west side of 400 W 1600 N, moved back to R8 Zoning allowing for more of a buffer behind my property between residential and future commercial or multifamily developments. This is a residential area and we want to keep it residential. Traffic is a problem that takes away from the residential feel. 400 West above 1600 North has become a major artery for Orem, Lindon and Pleasant Grove. The zoning corrections will help reduce the size and setbacks of the commercial development that is in the plans. The next concern is the existing traffic and future traffic on 400 West above 1600 N. Any development in the North East corner of the NVD should not be allowed unless it has access to State Street. Please Approve the NVD buffer Zones to be between the most restrictive re the 50’ setback (or more) or the setback equal to the height. Also the re-zoning of our 8 homes back to R8 as per our petition to the city. Thank you for your consideration. 9.3 PUBLIC HEARING - Amending the Current Fiscal Year 2020-2021 Budget None

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: The area of the North Village District is in need of your help. We would like to have the setback behind our houses changed from 50 feet to 100 feet. The additional 50 feet added on to this is NOT a lot of space. But it is enough that it would help us to be able to keep some semblance of a neighborhood. Jason and Ryan said in their letter to you that they applaud us for trying to preserve our neighborhood. However, they aren’t willing to budge on this issue. They think that the 50 foot setback is good enough. But, do you realize that they are not saying that nothing will be built in that 50 foot setback? They are saying that something that is 35 feet tall, could be built in that first 50 feet. The high density housing plan that is suppose to be kept on State Street and help to build up State Street, is not going to be on State Street at all. They are saying that it is going to start right at our back fences starting at 35 feet and then building up as it gets farther away. We are not against the North Village District being built. We realize that it is going to happen, and it could improve the city. However, we are asking you to work with us. We are asking you to help us preserve our neighborhoods just a little bit. Just adding an extra 50 feet to the setback behind the houses would help that. Even adding just an additional 25 feet to make it a 75 foot buffer would help us to preserve our neighborhood just a little more and keep the building height smaller near our fence lines. Having that little bit more space where something huge could not be so close to the houses would be the best thing in preserving a neighborhood. And that is what the State Street Master Plan was all about. It was created to help preserve neighborhoods and create more living space. But that is not what is happening right now. Plans are to build high density housing right next to residential. Right at the fence line to houses. There isn’t anything that is being put on State Street. I ask you, if this was being built right next to your houses, wouldn’t you want to have a little bit more of a buffer between it and you? Making the buffer 75-100 feet would guarantee that the building step up would be a little bit farther away from the homes. It would mean that we wouldn’t have a large structure right next to our backyards. It would mean that the 35 foot tall structure could still be able to be built there, but it would continue another 25-50 feet than is already planned. Think about it. 25-50 feet more. The size of one living room. That is the distance that we are asking for the height limits to be continued. Please help us add just a little bit more of a buffer to help us preserve our neighborhood. Please help us keep the original statement of using the State Street Master Plan to help preserve our neighborhoods true.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I have seen Phase 2 of the High-Density High Rise Housing Project that again affects 400 West in North Orem. This second project is a space from me, but Phase 1 is directly across the street from my residence. I do not understand the big rush to implement these housing projects, especially when they ‘bulldoze’ forward and ignore residents’ concerns. I have lived in an area, before I moved to Orem, where a high-density housing project was built directly behind my house. There was no buffer zone; the complex was literally six feet from my back fence. I used to be able to go into my backyard that was fenced, but with this housing project, I lost my privacy because people just looked out their window into my backyard. This Phase 2 project I see as a repeat of what I endured until I finally just had to sell my home where my family lived for thirty years because of this problem. If Orem City is going to continue to encourage high- density housing in residential areas, then it needs to create a buffer zone of 75 to 100 feet from adjacent home property lines. Many people have backyard patios, play areas for their families. High-rise housing robs them of their privacy, their enjoyment of an afternoon sunset. If these projects loom over residences, then in my opinion, they should be lower height as they near residential neighborhoods and houses. I watch traffic every morning come down 400 West to 1600 North. There are mornings when cars are backed up nearly to 2000 North. Phase 1 and 2 will inundate the area with traffic creating dangerous situations for families with children, pets, and just residents trying to gain access to the road in front of their homes. The speed limit on 400 West is 25 mph; I see cars exceed that limit all the time. Finally, there needs to be a 50 foot setback from homes that is nonstructural. Progress is a fact of life; I understand that; however, as a resident of Orem for thirty years, I should have the right to maintain my quality of living. I want to protect my home and continue the safety of my neighborhood. Increasing the ‘buffer zones’ and moving traffic access to State Street is one way of keeping a ‘good neighbor’ status between the city and its residents. Charles Tanner This is another silly problem to have placed in this area! It’s way too close to State st. And the quick light at 400 w. Just ridiculous to even have a meeting about it! Too much traffic on 1600 no. A very dangerous intersection already! To contend with!! I never wanted a left turn on 400 w the last time it was changed. Don’t slow !!!

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Please work hard to continue to develop more accessible housing in Orem. This is a wonderful place to live, and I believe many should be able to join the wonderful community here. I believe current proposals with setbacks detailed on the Knighton Architecture proposal dated 3.3.21 are appropriate, and further restriction discourages creation of this accessible housing Orem needs.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Your time, as well as mine, is valuable. I appreciate the attention given to Orem City residents concerns and our issues with the North Village District. I am new to understanding the current set-back regulations permitted. That being said, I have read and agree with what Stephanie Visnaw has written and presented to you in her letter and refer you to reread it. I ask that you please listen to the residents that voted you in, trusting that you would make moral and honest decisions on our behalf. Your decisions affect our daily lives. Thank you for your time.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Thank you, again, for taking the time to give attention to the North Village District and some of its challenges and concerns. Hopefully, you have had the opportunity to review the residents’ proposal and driving tour emailed to you earlier. Our hope is that this proposal and the real-life, visual examples of current setbacks has clarified the issue at hand, that residential homes need more protection and buffer from larger development in our area. The Planning Commission’s 50-foot setback proposal was tabled to further understand setbacks and the residents’ request to increase the setback to 100 feet. This 100-foot request is not as restricting as it appears. Rather, it gives guideline and direction to how property can be used – parking or the required 20% open space (Code of Ordinances 22-24-5-12), as well as providing an adequate buffer for adjacent residential property. The residents’ proposal includes a 50-foot “non-structure” area that can be addressed later. The main focus is the issue at hand - to increase the 50-foot setback to 100 feet, or a compromise of 75 feet, which hopefully the City Council will consider. This increased setback would still allow buildings of up to 35’ to be built within the first 100 feet (or 75-foot compromise), providing the necessary buffer that has not been achieved through zoning. Zoning in the North Village District uses the Edge Zone (NVD-E) as a transition from larger, commercial property to adjacent residential property. Being a transition zone, the Edge Zone should have a maximum height restriction to “feather” back from commercial and high-density housing, which is does not. Since Edge Zones do not have maximum height restrictions and allow high-density housing, an adequate buffer or setback is even more important. Increasing the proposed setback from 50 feet to 75, or even 100 feet, would provide a better buffer for these residential homes that abut Edge Zones.Increasing the already proposed 50-foot setback to 100, or even 75, would provide a more appropriate buffer in areas where Edge Zones abut residential. Again, this buffer area is not “dead space” but an area where structures can be up to 35 feet and where the required open space or parking could be directed. The North Village District is a narrow district with unique challenges. We hope the City Council will improve the Master Plan to accommodate the specific needs of this district. Thank you for taking the time to consider the residents in the North Village District. Residents would prefer the 100 foot setback - which still allows a 35 foot tall building. With a 75 or 100 foot setback - limiting up to 35' height is sufficient on those properties near residential or on smaller lots. A 35 foot tall building is still a significant height - especially on a smaller property like the corners in question. It's not "killing" development, but creating a transition, "feathering" back development with smaller buildings where appropriate and taller buildings where more property is available for buffering.

subject: general public comment
comment: Please keep Orem a "bedroom community". The high-rise projects are changing the face of our community and the desirability of living here. Orem is already such a hub of outside traffic coming to the malls and shopping centers. That's not bad per-say, but I don't need more traffic beyond our current traffic. I live off of 400 North, and often have to wait for a long procession of cars in order to cross at the crosswalk. This seems to be primarily because of traffic from Vineyard up to Orem. Summary: We don't need more residents or traffic.

subject: general public comment
comment: I understand the proposed high density apartment development in North Orem that fits under the provisions of the State Street Master Plan. I have heard the neighbors are pushing back about the transition from the neighborhoods to the developments along state street and I believe this is a part of the Master Plan that was not fully considered. I do recognize there are many natural buffers between SOME neighborhoods and what the plans calls for, but there are also many other areas where the plan has not fully taken into account the kind of transitions that preserve the integrity of the neighborhood. They are too abrupt and don’t make sense from a buffer perspective for state street either. These were some of issues raised when the master plan was adopted. How can they be acceptably addressed now so that we don’t have to have this type of issue every time a development occurs? The smaller parcels of property shouldn't have higher buildings on them anyways. If they are not large and are next to residentially zoned neighborhoods, then what's wrong with properties that cannot be developed.

subject: general public comment
comment: I see no place to access this "proposed" monstrosity. Plus, it will dwarf all the buildings around it, and you'll have another eyesore like the one on State Street at 350 South, with the silly name. It really doesn't seem to accomplish the 'Welcome to Orem' atmosphere you're going for.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I appreciate City Council member’s time and consideration on this matter. As a homeowner in the North Village District, I do not oppose the development of high-density housing that is in alignment with the ORIGINAL vision that was presented to us with appropriate access points and vibrant developments on State Street. The original vision looked great on paper but I believe this is the perfect time to reconsider its execution before it creates a greater problem in this area. We ask that you recognize that the desire of ONE developer to squeeze every last inch out of this landlocked property without proper infrastructure and access points would have a detrimental impact on thousands of property owners who live in the North Orem neighborhoods and those that drive through these intersections and not just those who live along 400 West. I agree with the proposal shared by Stephanie Visnaw and LaNeah Millet of increasing setbacks to 75 ft or even 100 ft from homeowners property lines with a 0-50 feet – zone identified as a “non- structure” area behind homes for the following reasons: NVD Edge zones do NOT have maximum height restrictions. Pictures were shared with City council members what potentially a 70 ft. building like Midtown 360 could look like from 50 ft. and 70 ft. views.Buildings can be built within that first 50 feet, just cannot exceed 35 feet. A 6 stories building 50ft away, starting at 35 ft. so close to homes it NOT protecting howmeowners and neighborhoods. It is extremely intrusive to homeowners living west and east of 400 West. The proposed 50-foot setback is NOT 50 feet of vacant, open land. A 0-50 feet – zone identified as a “non-structure” area behind homes with a 75 ft or 100 ft. would still allows for the development of the property with a parking lot, open space, and easement placement. City Planners would argue that our requests are more restrictive in nature, and the Mayor has said and I quote “if homeowners along 400 W. are against it then they should not have stayed”. I find this type of statement coming from our Mayor quite disheartening when some of these residents have lived along this street for generations! I would remind you when original plans of NVD were presented we were reassured by city planners that any large high density developments would remain on State Street and not engulf residential homes. NVD zone is different than other State street developments and setbacks must be addressed differently. It is closer to residential, smaller in size, and less commercial. This intersection is one of the most dangerous in Utah County (See Daily Herald, 2019), and 400 West is heavily trafficked. It’s important to highlight that the only ingress/ egress to this property is via only right turn onto 1600 N. No one is using the turnaround next to Quick quack to turn back westbound on 1600 N or to enter this property instead drivers use 400 West to make Uturns. Now, imagine the undrivable conditions a development so close to this intersection would create at this location We request that City Council considers appropriate setbacks to protect residential homes, and adequate access points to State Street to mitigate dangerous traffic conditions at this node. We fear that, if an increase of setbacks and limitations on height so close to homes is not granted, it will have a detrimental impact not only in this area but in other areas around our city where large developments are already taking place encroaching on residential areas and jeopardizing the safety of families in the neighborhoods and the preservation of the city we love.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I have read the response from Mayor Brunst to a neighbor. I hope each of you will read what the Mayor has to say about the proposed (and heavily contested) development at 1600 N and 400 W. What he said to this resident is what he is saying to each of us, who are also residents directly affected by the proposed development: • He claims the complex is “for condominiums to be sold and not for apartments … with 20 percent of affordable housing unit” [contained therein] o Selling a condo means absolutely NOTHING about it being occupied by the actual owner. Condos are bought as investment properties all the time, and then leased to occupants, the same as apartments. Being a condo doesn’t change a thing about its transitory nature within the community. Young families are not likely to have their starter home be in a high-rise condo. They find smaller/starter homes and townhomes in neighborhoods with parks, open spaces, other young families, newer amenities. This argument for helping young families build equity is false. o Putting in high-density and affordable housing within a stone’s throw of the State Liquor Store (some of the proposed property actually shares the parking lot with the State Liquor Store) is a BAD idea. We have repeatedly asked for studies about crime rates within close proximity of highdensity/affordable housing and the State Liquor Store, and still NOTHING has been provided by the developer nor the City of Orem. Unacceptable. o Orem City is already 40% rentals. FORTY PERCENT! • From Brunst directly: “I would ask you to consider what is reasonable – what if you were the other property owner – how would you want to be treated – what if you owned multiple homes on 400 West how would you want to be treated – have not all resudential (sp) homeowners known that they bordered commercial property along their back fence which would develop – and in fact if they are against this THEN THEY SHOULD NOT HAVE STAYED – we need to have fair property rights for all property owners … I believe that proper and fair compromises have been made – I would hope [you] would stop and consider what is fair for both sides equally.” (emphasis added) o This is NOT the language a Mayor should ever have, not privately and not to a resident being affected. How condescending, how insulting, how disgusting! This is spoken from a rich person living in CherApple about a rich developer living in the WordPerfect mansion community, ABOUT A NEIGHBORHOOD AND HOMEOWNERS THAT THEY ARE NOT PART OF. The audacity and insensitivity of a community leader to place ONE developer above what over 75+ families in just my immediate neighborhood have written and expressed discontent with. This should outrage everyone!!! There is no other way to say it. And for a rich person to simply suggest that a longtime resident of a neighborhood should just move away is appalling. Oh to have the financial freedom to do such a thing – only a rich person from CherApple could go so far. Oh to have the emotional lacking to simply leave friends and residents that we raise(d) our children with and mourned lost friends with because we see an undesirable circumstance arise. We residents have the right to defend our neighborhoods. The Mayor is supposed to stand up for our communities. He is supposed to lead out for all. Mayor Brunst’s words hold no compassion, no real desire for anything mutually beneficial. Give it up lessers, that’s what he’s asking. o I want an explanation from the Mayor about his choice of language, and also his relationship with the developer. He is saying, “I’m placing the rights of this one particular person over the rights of many, many others.” If the developer and the Mayor believe this project is so beneficial, then they can work to get this done in the neighborhoods they live in. (cue the outrage of the rich, safety-centered neighbors in CherApple and WordPerfect Park) The hypocrisy of the Mayor asking residents about their property rights of where they live versus the developer’s property rights of an investment property is breathtaking! o What compromises is the Mayor referring to? What has been offered for residents in this neighborhood? There aren't even sidewalks or gutter or lighting along some parts of 400 West. There are parts of an irrigation canal that have been open and unkempt FOR YEARS. What compromises have been made when basic street elements haven’t been provided? Is the Mayor receiving compromises personally? What consideration is he asking us to give up for things to be “fair for both sides equally” because having our traffic increase, our views ruined by 6-story buildings and potential increase in crime and property taxes seems like too much? What consideration has the developer given up to be “fair for both sides equally”? Seems quite unequal. I share the following from personal experience: • As a scout leader for Webelos Pack 876, we visited with Mayor Brunst on June 7, 2016. Our group asked the Mayor what the biggest energy problem facing Orem was (required question for the badge we were working on). Mayor Brunst responded that the Orem City Center offices and adjoining Library were the worst energy problem facing Orem. The office building had had “several” electrical fires, was not seismically sound, was not energy efficient. He laughingly called the building, “a bit of a tinderbox.” Our scouts discussed ways to fix the problem at meetings throughout the year. The following year we revisited the Mayor and asked the same question, hoping some new information could be shared about things being done to remedy the problem. Instead he changed the subject and talked about Orem water. I watched for information from the city for years, wondering when/if voting on bonds would come up. Nothing. When I saw the construction crews begin expansion of the new wing of the Orem City Offices and Library, I was physically sick. Why would anyone approve building a multi-million dollar facility onto an outdated “tinderbox”?! It defies fiscal responsibility and physical safety principles. • At the same meeting the Mayor said his favorite days as Mayor were groundbreaking ceremonies. Not opening new schools, not a student winning a state or national award, not safety and/or energy-efficient strides in government facilities, not improved family circumstances for all residents. No, this is a person who is out for himself and developers. This man is a not out for the good of the residents of Orem. We are a loooooong way from the “Most Livable City” status that Orem once boasted of.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I want to express my appreciation for the passion of Jason and Ryan as well as other city staff in working so hard to provide equitable solutions for all property owners - residential, commercial, or mixed use. I want to state that I am NOT against development of the state street corridor and I am NOT against growth and progress in our beautiful city. I just do not want it directly located in my backyard destroying the desirable Orem neighborhood residential feel. As a resident in the buffer zone on 400 West above 1600 North, I have a home and I want my property to be residential. Any buffer that limits the distance and elevation between me and commercial properties is extremely appreciated, the more the better. I do not want a developer to be able to build a skyrise next to my backyard. I would favor designs that support parking or common park uses to help buffer my home from tall development, also pushing tall buildings toward state street helps develop big & beautiful building fronts on state street where they are very ugly on my back yard property line. Additionally, I have huge concerns about traffic, parking, and access to a bottle necked property where large developments are being proposed. I trust that such a proposal would go through a good vetting process taking these concerns into consideration.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: Our neighborhood is asking you to create an ordinance that would provide a transition or buffer zone between our neighborhoods and high-rise/high density housing planned along State Street. We firmly believe that the intent of the State Street Master Plan is to place high-rise housing adjacent to State Street, and not along our back fence lines. As landscaping and parking will be required for any project built, we request you simply designate that the parking and landscaping required for such buildings should be located on the side of the development that abuts the homes—designate that area a non-structure. A nonstructure area would not impact the property rights of the commercial landowners. A good example is the Alpine Credit Union building. ACU placed the parking for their building behind the buildings and adjacent to the homes, thus creating a buffer. Parking and open green space will be a part of any commercial or residential development built in Orem. This isn’t an issue of limiting property use, just directing it. We affirm that the Districts were established to pull high-density housing out of single-family neighborhoods. We could reword that to say, the intent is to put high-density housing on State Street and the intent is to mitigate the impact of high-density housing on single-family homes. Our proposal of a wider, 100-foot setback fits within both of the objectives of mitigating impact, while still allowing business owners to develop their land. Property rights on both sides are being affected here. We feel our proposal of combining a setback, along with non-structure area guidelines, is a good balance for all property owners. Thank you for your efforts to understand this issue and I hope you will institute ordinances that will give builders the guidelines to create their projects in a way that will protect the property rights of the homeowners.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: The residents near the North Village area have not had due process with respect to the proposed development. The developer's agents never provided the comments from the original neighborhood meeting as promised. The development appears to have changed architects or designers as well. As neighbors, we are asking to be heard--rather than being asked to moved as was suggested by some of our elected representatives.

subject: general public comment
comment: A recent traffic study won't work since we are in Covid. You need one pre-Covid. Our neighborhood is insanely busy normally. We are toned down at the current moment. Please listen to us rather than listening to the dollar. And if you are going to compare fast food businesses you can only compare the business in Orem traffic not national traffic.

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I have some concerns about the large developments proposed on 1600 W. and 400 N. 1. 1600 N is already very narrow and crowded as you go East to access 1-15. I'm concerned that we are adding more residents to an area that isn't equipped to handle the current traffic needs. I request that the 1600 N access to I-15 be widen with more lanes before we add more residents. 2. I'm concerned about the increase of traffic in residential neighborhoods. I request parking lot access to these developments be off State Street or where 1600 N is business zoned, not in residential neighborhoods like 400 N or west 1600 N. 3. I'm concerned about the proposed 6 story height of these developments so close to residential neighborhoods and by businesses that are single or two story structures. I request setbacks of 75 feet from residential homes and structure height lower as it approaches existing homes.

subject: general public comment
comment: We moved to Orem in 1969. To put that into perspective we moved here before they had a traffic signal light at the intersection of 1600 North and State Street. We have lived on 1600 North this entire time. We have watched a quiet country road turn into an extremely busy city street. We built our home on property that my Grandfather owned and farmed until his death, so it is meaningful to me, and is the main reason why we have stayed in Orem. When we wanted to build our home we were only able to do so, if we put in the sidewalk, curb and gutter along our property, and it had to be done at our expense. Later on the City put in the sidewalk, curb and gutter all along 1600 North at the Cities expense (our taxes) for all those who didn't have it. Then the street became so busy that the City had to come in on our frontage to widen the road, and they tore up my sidewalk without any consideration. That's not the end of the story! A second time they widened the road and again came in on our frontage. This time we were left without a pull over in front of our house. Our newspaper delivery person told us it was to dangerous for him to deliver the paper to us , and we would need to move our paper box. So after 50 years we stopped taking the newspaper. And now we have the City figuring to allow a development that will further frustrate the people who live in our area with even busier streets! There are certain times of the day when we can't get out of our driveway as it is! Sadly this is only one of the problematic issues we will be dealing with. Orem City, we have put up with a lot over the years since we have been here, but this one is just asking to much!

subject: North Village District zoning/setbacks
comment: I want to thank the city planning folks for making this recommendation. I am happy that the council passed the 75' setback. The residential rezone adds an additional setback to the height that will help preserve our privacy and somewhat of a neighborhood feel. The developer has rights to develop his property, and he purchased bottlenecked property with no real access to State street. Development should be pushed toward state street. He needs realistic plans for the property he purchased.
